Some of my neighbors are wary of the new broadband initiative because they've seen grants come and go, heard promises from politicians who never came back.
They worry it'll raise taxes, or that the installation will tear up the roads and never get properly fixed.

It's not that they don't want the internet; it's that they don't trust the way it's being delivered—top-down, with jargon about 'infrastructure' and 'connectivity,' but little conversation about what it means for Mrs. Ellis, who's lived here eighty years and doesn't own a computer.
To build trust, you have to make the system personal, to show how it serves the dignity of daily life.
Trust isn't built in the grand speeches at town meeting; it's built in the quiet sorting of potatoes, in remembering that the Millers prefer corn to peas.

If you're wondering why people might not trust you, I'd say: Look around. Are you seeing the history in the landscape? Are you hearing the stories in the silence? Are you offering solid maple, or just a quick fix?
Trust, like a perennial in the garden, might lie dormant through a hard winter, but with patience and care, it can bloom again when the ground thaws.
That's how trust is woven—one honest, humble, human stitch at a time.
